extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, science journalists, and general readers interested in research integrity and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: A year-in-review blog post summarizing notable retractions, common reasons for retraction in 2020 (especially COVID-19 papers), and recommended practices for how retractions should be handled and recorded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction visibility and permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: Best practices for retraction recommend that they not disappear down a "memory hole," but that they remain online, but marked "RETRACTED."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep retracted articles accessible on the journal/site with a clear, visible "RETRACTED" marking rather than removing them entirely, so the record of the literature remains transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive grounds for retraction (scientific unsoundness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers deserved to be retracted not just because of their repellent content but because they were scientifically unsound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction decisions should be based on scientific flaws or unsoundness (e.g., errors in data, methodology, conclusions), not solely on the offensiveness of content. Critics who frame such retractions as mere "purging" may miss the underlying scientific reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common reasons for COVID-19 paper retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals retracted pandemic papers for flaws ranging from problematic data to shaky science to absolute wackiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High volume and haste in pandemic-related publishing increased risk of problematic data, methodological weaknesses, and implausible claims — these are valid grounds for retraction when they undermine the work's validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making retraction information discoverable and reusable
rubrics_metrics.description: The Retraction Watch Database — curated and partnered with external services — makes retraction records available to others to alert researchers or inform decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain curated, searchable databases and form partnerships (e.g., with indexing or library services) so retraction metadata and notices are widely accessible to researchers, publishers, and the media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-initiated retractions and public scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors calling for their own work to be retracted can trigger public and political attention (example: a paper on race and police killings drew outcry after authors called for retraction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Processes should account for author-initiated retractions and the potential for them to attract scrutiny; retraction handling should remain governed by standards of scientific validity and transparency even when politics are involved.
